name: The Hindsight Bias
statement: Once you know how it turned out, it feels as if you knew it all along.
meaning: Hindsight bias is the tendency, after an event has happened, to see it as having been more predictable or even inevitable than it really was. Knowing the outcome, people overestimate how well they could have foreseen it, and remember themselves as having expected it. It is the I-knew-it-all-along effect, and it quietly rewrites our sense of what we believed before we learned how things turned out.
mechanism: Several processes combine. Once the outcome is known, we may misremember our earlier prediction, shifting it toward what actually happened. We also make sense of the result by reinterpreting the prior evidence into a tidy causal story, and the ease of building that story is misread as foreseeability, a creeping determinism. Motivational needs for a predictable, orderly world and a wish to have known push in the same direction. The person is usually unaware the memory has changed, so the revised belief feels like the original.

examples.text: Only once a team has lost do fans declare they knew it would, and Monday-morning quarterbacking treats the right call as obvious in hindsight.
In medicine and law, a physician's diagnosis or a defendant's conduct is judged more harshly once a bad outcome is known, since the harm now seems foreseeable.
In the founding study, people who had estimated the odds of outcomes of Nixon's 1972 visits to Beijing and Moscow later recalled their estimates as closer to what actually happened.

variants.name: Three levels
variants.text: Memory distortion, misremembering an earlier judgement; inevitability, believing the event had to happen; and foreseeability, believing one personally could have foreseen it, from lower to higher.

variants.name: Outcome bias
variants.text: The related tendency to judge a decision by how it turned out rather than by what was known at the time; distinct from hindsight bias but often reinforcing it.

whyItMatters: It distorts how we learn from experience, since outcomes that seem to have been obvious teach the wrong lessons and breed overconfidence. It shapes judgements of negligence and malpractice in law and medicine, where foreseeability standards are especially vulnerable, and it colours history and investing by making the past look more inevitable than it was. Recognising it is a first step toward fairer retrospective judgement.

working.text: write down what you expect before the outcome, since memory of your earlier judgement will drift toward what happened.

working.lead: Judge decisions by the foresight available
working.text: evaluate a choice by what was known at the time, not by how it turned out, to counter outcome-driven blame.
deliberately consider how else things could have gone, which loosens the sense that the actual result was inevitable.

limits: It is a robust, well-replicated effect across many domains, but it is not universal: very surprising or seemingly impossible outcomes can sometimes reduce or even reverse it, and its size varies with the experimental paradigm. It is distinct from outcome bias, which concerns judging a decision's quality by its result, and from the curse of knowledge, though the three interrelate. The memory change is typically genuine and unconscious rather than boasting.
misreadings: It is not lying or bragging; the shift in memory is usually real and the person is unaware of it. It is not the same as outcome bias, which is judging a decision by its result rather than distorting one's sense of prior predictability. And it does not mean the outcome truly was predictable; it means it only feels that way once known.
origin: Established by Baruch Fischhoff and Ruth Beyth in 1975, whose studies of remembered probabilities and of judgement under outcome knowledge defined the effect and its creeping-determinism mechanism.

sources.text: Fischhoff & Beyth, "I knew it would happen," Organizational Behavior and Human Performance 13 (1975): 1-16. — the remembered-probabilities demonstration.
